headline: Destro's Smart Software Helps Robots and Warehouse Workers Work Together

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A company called Destro made something new to help robots and people work together. Destro does not build robots itself. Instead, it makes smart computer programs that tell both robots and human workers what to do in big warehouses. These warehouses sort packages from trucks and send them to new trucks. This is hard work to organize. Destro's programs act like a helpful brain that tells everyone, robots and people, exactly what job to do next. A company called Yusen Logistics tried out Destro's idea. They used small robots that carry carts full of packages. While workers unload trucks and fill carts, the robots find the full carts and bring them to the right place. This helps the warehouse work faster and with less confusion, and workers do not need to use paper lists anymore. Destro's system worked so well that Yusen wants to use many more robots at another location. Destro plans to bring this same idea to other warehouses across the country. Some investors liked this plan so much that they gave Destro eight million dollars to grow. This shows that sometimes the smartest technology idea is not a new robot, but a better way for robots and humans to work as a team.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Most robotics companies try to build cool new robots. But a startup called Destro took a different approach. Instead of designing robots, Destro built smart software that helps robots and human workers cooperate smoothly, especially in busy warehouses. The founder, Manthan Pawar, believes understanding customers' real problems matters more than fancy robot designs. Destro's software works in a process called 'cross-docking.' This is when workers unload goods from one truck and sort them into new loads for other trucks. It's complicated because trucks, carts, and people all need to move at the right times. Destro's system, called Mothership, directs everything: it tells workers which items go where, and tells robots which full carts to pick up and deliver. A shipping company called Yusen Logistics tested this system with just three cart-moving robots. It worked so well that Yusen now plans to use 26 robots at that location, plus 17 more robots at a new warehouse in Southern California. Other robot companies Yusen tried couldn't handle the whole job. One could only move carts, and another needed a human to manage everything. Destro stood out because its system could organize the entire process by itself. Because of this success, investors gave Destro $8 million to expand its idea to other warehouses. However, Destro's approach might not work as well for jobs needing more delicate movements, like handling fragile items, since current robot technology isn't advanced enough yet for those precise tasks. Still, this story shows an important lesson: sometimes the smartest technology solutions come from figuring out how machines and humans can work together, not just building a new machine.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: A new startup named Destro is taking an unusual approach to robotics: instead of building robots, it builds the software that tells robots and human workers what to do. The company just announced $8 million in funding after operating secretly for a while, and it believes its strategy will help it succeed where other robotics companies struggle. Founder Manthan Pawar argues that many robotics companies focus on flashy engineering instead of solving real customer problems. Destro's software works in logistics warehouses, specifically for 'cross-docking'—a process where workers unload goods from incoming trucks and sort them into new combinations for outgoing trucks. This requires careful coordination between people, robot carts, and trucks. Destro's 'Mothership' system manages that coordination by directing both the robots and the human workers, removing the need for paper checklists and confusing manual planning. The idea took shape after a partnership with Richard Brunelle, an automation director at Yusen Logistics, a major shipping company. He convinced Destro to adapt its original technology (built for sorting packages) to fit the cross-docking problem instead. After testing the software with just three cart-carrying robots at one facility, the results impressed Yusen enough that they're expanding to 26 robots there and starting a new pilot with 17 robots at another location. Yusen chose Destro over two other robotics companies. One competitor's robots could only move carts short distances but couldn't manage loading or unloading. Another had good tracking tools but still needed a human to manage the whole operation manually. Destro's system stood out because it could direct the entire workflow independently. Pawar hopes to replicate this successful setup at thousands of similar warehouses across the country. Investors from Base10 Partners and Bonfire Ventures were convinced enough by this plan to lead Destro's funding round. However, the article notes a challenge ahead: many warehouse tasks require delicate hand movements that today's robots and AI models still struggle to perform well. It remains unclear whether major robotics and AI companies will let smaller companies like Destro use their advanced tools, or if they'll try to control that market themselves. Still, Brunelle emphasizes that automation should only be added when it solves real problems—not just because the technology seems impressive.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Destro, a robotics startup, just emerged from stealth mode with $8 million in seed funding, and its strategy stands out from most competitors in the field. Rather than designing new robots or advanced AI models to control robotic movement, Destro built a software layer that coordinates both robots and human workers within logistics operations. Founder Manthan Pawar, who has years of experience in supply chain robotics, argues that many robotics startups focus too much on impressive engineering feats rather than truly understanding customer problems. Destro's approach centers on 'cross-docking,' a common warehouse process where incoming trucks are unloaded and their contents re-sorted into new combinations for outgoing delivery trucks. This requires precise coordination between workers, mobile robot carts, and shipping schedules. Destro's 'Mothership' operating system manages this entire workflow, directing which items human workers should sort and where robots should transport finished loads, replacing inefficient manual planning and paperwork. The concept evolved through collaboration with Richard Brunelle, an automation director at Yusen Logistics, a major international shipping company. Destro had originally built its technology for picking and packing—organizing mixed items into single packages—but Brunelle recognized the underlying challenge was similar to his own cross-docking problem and convinced Destro to adapt its system. After a successful pilot using three cart-moving robots (built by Miva Robotics and guided by Destro's vision-based AI models) at one Pacific Northwest facility, Yusen is now expanding to 26 robots at that site and launching a second pilot with 17 robots in Southern California. Notably, Yusen evaluated two other robotics companies before choosing Destro. One offered robots that could transport carts but couldn't handle loading or unloading tasks. The other provided fleet management tools but still required constant human oversight to coordinate operations. Destro won the contract because its software could autonomously manage the entire process from start to finish. Pawar now hopes to replicate this model at thousands of similar warehouses nationwide, a scalability plan that persuaded investors Base10 Partners and Bonfire Ventures to lead the funding round. Despite this early success, the article raises a significant challenge: tasks requiring fine motor skills and dexterity—like handling delicate or irregularly shaped items—remain difficult for today's robots and AI systems. It's also uncertain whether companies developing advanced robotic hands or humanoid robots will share their technology with smaller companies like Destro, or attempt to dominate the logistics market themselves. Still, Brunelle stresses that automation should be adopted only when it solves genuine operational problems, not simply because a technology seems futuristic or exciting.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Destro, a robotics startup that just emerged from stealth with $8 million in seed funding, is challenging a common assumption in the robotics industry: that success depends on building better robots or more sophisticated AI models for physical manipulation. Instead, Destro has built an 'intelligence layer'—software that coordinates both robotic systems and human workers within complex logistics environments. Founder Manthan Pawar, a robotics engineer with roughly eight years of supply chain industry experience, contends that many robotics companies prioritize technically impressive engineering over deeply understanding customer pain points, and he believes this focus on real operational problems is why Destro is outcompeting rivals, even as the company approaches profitability by year's end. The company's core use case involves 'cross-docking,' a logistics process in which goods arriving on one truck are unloaded and immediately re-sorted into new combinations for outgoing delivery trucks, without ever being placed into long-term storage. This process demands tight coordination among human workers, mobile equipment, and shifting schedules. Destro's 'Mothership' operating system manages this entire orchestration, directing human workers on what to sort while simultaneously guiding robotic carts on delivery routes—eliminating inefficient paper-based tracking systems in the process. This application emerged through a partnership with Richard Brunelle, automation director for Yusen Logistics' American operations, who oversees automation efforts across roughly 30 facilities. Destro's technology was originally designed for a different logistics challenge: pick-and-pack operations, where varied items are combined into single shipping packages. Brunelle recognized structural similarities between that problem and his own cross-docking challenges, and persuaded Destro to adapt its existing tools. Following a successful pilot at one Pacific Northwest facility using three cart-moving robots—built by Miva Robotics and controlled through Destro's vision-based AI system, which relies on open-weight vision-language-action models capable of interpreting camera footage to guide robotic movement—Yusen is now scaling to a full deployment of 26 robots at that site, alongside a new 17-robot pilot in Southern California. Significantly, Yusen had evaluated two other established robotics companies before selecting Destro. One offered robots limited to point-to-point cart transportation without loading or unloading capability. The other provided fleet management software but still required human staff to manually orchestrate operations. Destro differentiated itself by autonomously managing the full workflow end-to-end. Pawar envisions replicating this cross-docking model across thousands of similar warehouse facilities nationally, a scalability argument that persuaded investors Base10 Partners and Bonfire Ventures to lead the funding round, with additional backing from CoFound Partners. The article does note meaningful uncertainties ahead. Tasks requiring fine dexterity and manipulation remain a significant technical hurdle; current generic robot hardware and open-source AI models have not yet proven reliable for such nuanced physical tasks. Additionally, it remains unclear whether companies developing foundational AI models, advanced robotic hands, or general-purpose humanoid robots will make those technologies available to intermediary companies like Destro, or whether they will instead attempt to vertically integrate and capture that business themselves. Pawar remains confident that his company occupies a durable and valuable position in the robotics technology stack. Brunelle, meanwhile, offers a grounded perspective on automation adoption generally, noting that new technology should be deployed only when it solves genuine operational problems, rather than being implemented simply because it appears innovative or futuristic.

questions: Do you think it's smarter for a company to focus on making robots and humans work well together instead of building fancier robots? Why or why not?
How might jobs in warehouses or stores near you change if more companies started using systems like Destro's to guide both workers and robots?
The article mentions that delicate tasks are still hard for robots to do. Can you think of jobs in your community that might be difficult to automate, and why?
